tier_reason: First-party README numbers only: the APL code is public (README and src/{slow,procfn,windowed,split,mem-split}), but there is no timing harness, the Dyalog version is not stated, the wc build flags are unknown (macOS-shipped binary) and the CPU is given only as '2.2 GHz Intel Core i7', so it falls short of A; no independent or peer-reviewed measurement exists.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Array-arithmetic version: 3.36 s on the first run, then 2.75, 2.34 and 2.36 s; windowed-reduction (2</) version: 3.33 s on the first run, then about 1.85 s; versus macOS wc user times of 5.345 to 5.549 s on the same 1.661 GB file. First naive partition-based APL version: 32.97 s. That is about 2.9-3.0x for the windowed version on warm runs and about 1.6-1.7x on its first run (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Counting lines, words and characters of one 1.661 GB text file (big.txt from Chris Penner's Haskell wc post, repeated), read in 256 KB blocks, timed with the dfns user-defined timing operator in Dyalog APL (wall time) against the time utility on the macOS wc (user time).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Dyalog APL interpreter (free personal copy, version not stated); wc is the binary shipped with macOS (Apple text_cmds), build flags unknown.
corrections.hardware: 2.2 GHz Intel Core i7 (exact model not stated), 8 GB 1600 MHz DDR3, 11-inch early-2015 MacBook Air
corrections.caveats: Mixed measurements: APL figures are wall-clock times from a timing operator, wc figures are user CPU times from time; wc's wall time is not reported (for a single-threaded wc it can only be equal or higher, so this mix does not favour APL, but the comparison is still not like for like). The fast APL figures are warm-cache repeat runs; the first runs are 3.33-3.36 s. Single file, single machine, no variance, no harness script. Not the same work: the APL version treats bytes 10, 11, 12 and 13 as line ends (so CRLF counts as two lines) and a fixed six-byte whitespace set, while wc counts only '\n' and calls the locale-aware iswspace() on every byte in a scalar loop (Apple text_cmds wc/wc.c, current source; the 2019 macOS build was not checked). wc build flags unknown, so equal optimisation cannot be shown. The README itself says faster wc versions likely exist. The code is BSD-2-Clause but needs the proprietary Dyalog interpreter (free for personal use) to run.
corrections.why_faster: Whole-array primitives over 256 KB blocks: one membership test (data in whitespace set) yields a boolean vector, +/ sums newline flags, and the 2</ windowed reduction counts word boundaries, so the per-element work runs inside the interpreter's compiled primitive loops; Dyalog stores Booleans one bit per element and has SIMD boolean algorithms (APL Wiki and a Dyalog '16 talk, search snippets only). The macOS wc instead runs a scalar per-byte loop that branches on each byte and calls iswspace() per byte (Apple text_cmds wc/wc.c). The win is the interpreter's vectorised primitives against a scalar locale-aware C utility, not APL codegen beating -O3 C on the same algorithm.

notes: README numbers match the record; metadata checked on github.com (BSD-2-Clause, 7 stars, 0 forks, not a fork, not archived, 7 commits, last commit 2019-10-26 'Added Windowed Reductions', so abandoned). Shortcomings to record: baseline is the stock macOS wc (unknown flags, not shown to be -O3) doing different work (locale-aware iswspace per byte, '\n'-only line count) with a scalar loop; APL wall time against wc user time; warm-cache best runs; single file, no variance; language-level claim not supported because same_algorithm is false. aplwiki.com was unreachable (ENOTFOUND), so the bit-packing statement is from search snippets only.
